name: Singing lessons
lead: Singing lessons are instruction in vocal technique from a voice teacher, covering breath support, phonation, resonance, articulation and range.[1] In looksmaxxing culture they are mentioned as a way to gain voice control and range, including a deeper or more resonant speaking voice.

Wikipedia describes singing training as systematic practice of exercises for warm-ups, range extension, dynamics and agility, with teachers helping students match internal sensations to the sound produced.[2] Research on lessons has examined well-being, respiratory health and voice measures; no studies were found testing lessons for changing speaking pitch for appearance.
infobox: Studied for wellbeing and respiratory health; none for appearance

paras: Voice teachers usually start students in a comfortable middle range and avoid early classification, expanding range gradually.[1] Teaching approaches range from mechanistic, focusing on physical parts, to image-based, and many teachers combine them.[1] Vocal pedagogy dates in organised form to 13th-century monastic teachers and was shaped later by bel canto and 20th-century physiology-based teachers.[1][2]

A 2003 study of eight amateur and eight professional singers measured heart-rate variability and blood markers such as cortisol, oxytocin and TNF-alpha before and after a singing lesson, to explore effects on well-being.[3] A randomised trial compared eight weeks of singing classes with a film club in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, assessing health status, breathing control and exercise measures.[4] A 2018 literature review examined singing lessons for respiratory health.[5]

A 2010 study compared 36 untrained and 30 trained vocalists on the Dysphonia Severity Index and components such as maximum phonation time and highest phonational frequency.[6] A 2014 study examined the influence of vocal training and acting experience on voice quality and emotional genuineness.[7] No studies found testing singing lessons for deepening the speaking voice or for appearance.

timeline.event: Johannes de Garlandia and Jerome of Moravia describe the first known systematic approach to voice teaching.[1]
Giovanni Camillo Maffei's treatise links voice physiology to singing theory.[1]
William Vennard publishes Singing: The Mechanism and the Technic.[2]

card.summary: Lessons in vocal technique for control and range; studied for wellbeing and lungs, not for changing how your voice looks or sounds in speech.
card.note: No studies on lessons for deepening the speaking voice.

quick.overview:
Singing lessons teach breath support, resonance, articulation and range through guided exercises with a voice teacher.

Studies have looked at wellbeing, respiratory health and voice measures in singers; none tests lessons for appearance goals.
quick.mechanism: Teachers help students link internal sensations to the sound produced and extend range gradually from a comfortable middle range.
quick.risks: Singing sources note that overusing chest voice on high notes can cause forcing and may lead to vocal deterioration.
